title: How to Make Chef Ranveer Brar's Kashmiri Chicken Kathi Roll at Home
excerpt: The celebrity chef's 30-minute recipe pairs spice-marinated chicken thighs with two homemade chutneys, wrapped in a soft roti that traces its roots to Kolkata's Nizam's restaurant.
body:
• Chef Ranveer Brar shares a Kashmiri chicken kathi roll recipe that can be prepared in under 30 minutes at home
  • The recipe uses chicken thighs marinated with Kashmiri spices including degi red chilli powder, fennel powder and mustard oil
  • Two chutneys — onion (pyaz ki chutney) and radish (mooli ki chutney) with walnuts and curd — accompany the roll
  • The kathi roll traces its origins to Kolkata's Nizam's restaurant in the 1930s, where kebabs were first wrapped in parathas for customers on the go

Few Indian street foods have traveled as far as the kathi roll. Born in the lanes around Kolkata's New Market in the 1930s, when Nizam's restaurant first wrapped skewer-roasted kebabs in flaky parathas for hurried customers, the roll has since become a staple across India and in diaspora kitchens from New York to London. Chef Ranveer Brar's Kashmiri chicken kathi roll builds on that tradition with a regional twist, substituting the classic Mughlai spicing for the aromatic warmth of Kashmiri cuisine.

The Dough

The wrapping starts with equal parts whole wheat flour and refined flour — one cup of each. Salt, a teaspoon of sugar, half a teaspoon of vinegar and water are kneaded into a semi-soft dough. A teaspoon of oil, a quarter teaspoon each of baking soda and baking powder are then folded in and the mixture is kneaded until smooth. The dough is divided into lemon-sized balls, rolled into semi-thick rotis and cooked on a medium-heat tawa until done on both sides.

The Chicken Marination

One kilogram of chicken thighs forms the protein base. The marination draws directly from Kashmiri cooking: ginger-garlic paste, coriander powder, cumin powder, a pinch of garam masala, degi red chilli powder and fennel powder create the spice profile. Gram flour adds body to the coating and helps the marinade cling to the meat. Vinegar and two to three tablespoons of hot mustard oil bring the sharpness and depth that distinguish this roll from its Kolkata original.

The marinated pieces are cooked in a tablespoon or two of oil in a pan until tender, then set aside while the chutneys come together.

Two Chutneys, Two Textures

The pyaz ki chutney is a quick, no-cook preparation: sliced onions tossed with salt, vinegar, degi red chilli powder and cumin powder. The result is crunchy, acidic and designed to cut through the richness of the spiced meat.

The mooli ki chutney requires more layering. Sliced, grated and leafy parts of radish are combined with crushed walnuts, degi red chilli powder, chopped green chilli, fresh coriander leaves and cumin seeds. A tablespoon of oil and three-quarters of a cup of beaten curd bring everything together into a cool, textured condiment that balances the roll's heat. The walnut addition is a distinctly Kashmiri touch, lending a subtle nuttiness that complements the fennel in the chicken marinade.

"Soft roti, juicy chicken, and the rich flavours of Kashmiri spices, paired with onion and radish chutney — kathi roll is one of the most popular and flavourful Indian street-style wraps."

Assembly and Serving

The roll comes together in seconds. A cooked roti is laid on a flat surface, spread with mooli ki chutney, topped with pieces of cooked chicken and finished with a generous helping of pyaz ki chutney. It is rolled tightly to form the kathi shape, transferred to a serving platter and garnished with a coriander sprig. Both chutneys are served alongside for dipping.

The preparation time is 10 to 15 minutes and the cooking time is 15 to 20 minutes, making this a viable weeknight dinner for two to four people.

From Kolkata's Streets to Global Kitchens

The kathi roll takes its name from the Bengali word for stick — a reference to the bamboo skewers (kathi) that Nizam's adopted in 1964 to replace the heavy iron ones used originally, as demand for the snack grew. The format began as a mutton kebab wrapped in a paratha and has since expanded to include everything from paneer to egg-layered meats and even seafood.

For diaspora cooks, recipes like Brar's offer a way to recreate a taste that is deeply familiar but often hard to find done well outside India. The Kashmiri inflection — the fennel, the mustard oil, the walnut-radish chutney — adds a layer of regional specificity that elevates the roll beyond its street-food origins into something worth making deliberately at home.
nri_angle: A home-friendly recipe that lets diaspora cooks recreate an iconic Indian street food with Kashmiri regional flavours often unavailable outside India.
